food.text: Street food became an integral part of Chinese food culture in the 7th century, during the Tang dynasty. Eating on the go was already a lasting feature of daily life well over a thousand years ago.

The Cold Food Festival took its name from a tradition of not lighting any fire, even to prepare food. By the 7th century, under the Tang dynasty, it had grown into an occasion across East Asia for commemorating and venerating ancestors.

Dairy products were common in the Tang dynasty, but they came to be associated with foreign cultures. The source explains that this association is why cheese and milk are largely absent from the later Chinese diet.

The Cold Food Festival's fire ban once ran at midwinter for as long as a month, and the hardship it caused killed many people. According to the Book of the Later Han, people rich and poor kept a taboo on lighting fires, lest they anger the spirit of Jie Zhitui, and many of the old and young died every year because of the hardship. Huan Tan noted that people kept the taboo even when gravely ill. Repeated attempts were made to ban it. By the end of the Three Kingdoms period it was limited to three days in spring, and under the Tang ancestral observance was limited to a single day, now the Tomb-Sweeping Festival.
The first recipes for bing, the flat wheat-flour breads and doughy foods of China, appeared in the sixth century. They were recorded in an agricultural text called the Qimin Yaoshu.

Among the traditional cold foods eaten during the Cold Food Festival was lǐlào, a kind of congee. It was flavored with apricot pits and malt sugar, and needed no fire on the day when fires were forbidden.

A southern fire-avoidance custom lasted as late as the 10th century. Residents of the area avoided fire on the day of the death of the Yue king Mi, who was supposedly beheaded during a battle with Yao, yet his headless body stayed atop his horse all the way back to "Wu Village", where he was buried. Mi and Yao were actually princes of the old Yue royal family fighting over the successor state of Minyue. People avoided fire as a mark of respect to his spirit.

art.text: The Mogao Grottoes at Dunhuang, begun in the Northern Wei dynasty (386–534), consist of more than 700 caves. Of these, 492 have murals on their walls, totalling more than 45,000 square meters of painting.

The Tang dynasty was a golden age of Chinese civilization, with significant developments in culture, art, and literature, particularly poetry. Its capital, Chang'an (modern Xi'an), was a cosmopolitan hub of trade and foreign merchants.

Under the Tang dynasty (618–907 AD), the performing arts became popular in the emperor's court, and the acts became more refined. Later they lost favor at court and moved back to the common people, with most performers working in the street.
The early caves at the Mogao Grottoes show painting styles influenced by India and the West. From the Tang dynasty (618–906 CE), the murals began to reflect a unique Chinese painting style.
The Mogao murals are very broad in content. They include Buddha statues, paradise, angels, important historical events, and even donors, the people who paid for the paintings.
Chinese paper cutting, called jianzhi, has roots in China in the 6th century. It is attributed to Cai Lun during the Han dynasty and is a type of folk art.
Chinese knotting began as a form of folk art in the Tang and Song dynasties. This decorative handicraft creates patterned knots, and it was later popularized in the Ming.

Chinese pottery may have reached the Muslim world through war. After the Arabs defeated the Chinese at the Battle of Talas in 751, it has been argued that imprisoned Chinese potters and paper makers taught the Muslims their arts.

In the 800s, Chinese stoneware and porcelain reached the Abbasids. This was part of the first phase of Chinese pottery influence on Islamic ceramics, which began with contact at the Battle of Talas in 751.

war.text: In 648, the Tang envoy Wang Xuance led an army against Arunasva, who had seized the throne of Kannauj in India after his forces had killed or captured Wang's earlier mission. His force was made up of 1,200 Tibetan soldiers and over 7,000 Nepalese cavalrymen, supplied by Songtsen Gampo and Narendradeva. According to the Old Book of Tang, the fighting lasted three days and ended with the troops led by Wang overpowering their enemies.

In July 751, Tang and Abbasid armies clashed at the Talas River over control of the regions around the Syr Darya. The Tang army under Gao Xianzhi was defeated by an Abbasid army under Ziyad ibn Salih and Karluk mercenaries, who attacked the Tang rear while the Abbasids struck the front. Out of an estimated 10,000 or 20,000 Tang troops, fewer than 2,000 made it back, and Arabic sources put Chinese dead at 45,000 to 50,000 with 20,000 to 25,000 captured. The defeat ended Tang influence in Transoxiana and halted Tang westward expansion.

In 647, Wang Xuance reached Kannauj to find that Harsha had died and his minister Arunasva had usurped the throne. The new ruler received the mission badly, and his forces attacked it. Everyone was either killed or captured except Wang and his second-in-command Jiang Shiren, who escaped overnight to Nepal.

Songtsen Gampo built the Tibetan Empire by overwhelming the tribes around the Tibetan plateau, raiding Chinese towns and subjugating the Licchavis of Nepal. In 641 he then married Princess Wencheng, sealing a marriage alliance with the Tang dynasty.

Sources differ on whether the Karluks defected to the Abbasids at Talas or were Abbasid allies from the start. Afterward the Karluk Yabghus sent missions to the Tang in 752, and in 753 they submitted to the army of Cheng Qianli. They accepted appointment as Tang bridle officials.

The Tibetan Empire attacked China while its army also conquered territory in the Hindu Kush and Pamir Mountains. Under Harun al-Rashid, the Abbasids allied with the Tang and Uyghurs against the Tibetans, and the Uyghurs fought the Tibetans along the Silk Road.

After the battle, Arunasva fled the city but Jiang captured him. Wang returned to China with Arunasva as his captive and was granted the title "Grand Master for the Closing Court". Arunasva remained in China until his death and was given posthumous honors, and a statue of him was placed on the avenue leading to Taizong's tomb in the Zhao Mausoleum.

The article names two outcomes of the 648 battle. The Tang display of military power may have led Indian kingdoms to explore military ties with China. The Tibetan Empire also moved into the region Harsha had controlled, taking advantage of the political vacuum.

After Talas, the caliph sent an envoy to the Tang emperor, who arrived in December 752 to negotiate restoring diplomatic relations. Abu Muslim took 5,000 Chinese prisoners, according to al-Maqdisi, and Chinese prisoners captured at Talas in 751 are said to have introduced papermaking to the peoples of West Asia, although several findings dispute this account. Du Huan, captured by the Abbasid army at Talas, recorded that Chinese prisoners of war living on Abbasid territory practiced crafts such as silk weaving.

Sources place the 648 battle at Chabuheluo, believed to be Champaran, on the banks of the river Qiantuowei, believed to be the Gandaki River. According to the Old Book of Tang, over 3,000 people were beheaded and more than 10,000 died by drowning after jumping into the water. Another 2,000 men and women were captured, along with over 30,000 cows and horses.

In late 753, the Karluks captured Abuz Yabghu, a Tang general of Turkic descent who had defected to the Tongluo chief in 743. As a reward, the Karluk Yabghu Tun Bilga was given the title "Khagan of the Turgish" on 22 October.

Iron weapons continued to be exported to Tibet and China along the Silk Roads between Kuqa and Aksu near the Tarim Basin. Arabic sources record that in the 10th century Aksu and Fergana had markets for arms traders.

literature.text: Chinese literature counts the Tang dynasty (618 to 907) as one of its golden ages of poetry, alongside the earlier Han dynasty. The Tang left a body of verse that later poets kept returning to.
Widespread woodblock printing was introduced in China during the Tang dynasty. It spread written knowledge rapidly throughout the country, changing how texts reached readers.

From the 6th to the 9th centuries, Chinese was one of several classical languages inherited from earlier ages that stayed in active use, alongside Sanskrit, Latin, Greek, Persian and Hebrew. In Tang China this meant Literary Chinese.
A pilgrim to India named Xuanzang completed the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions in 646. The work is counted among the early Chinese writings that fed into later Chinese fiction.
tags: Great Tang Records on the Western Regions

literature.text: Miscellaneous Morsels from Youyang was one of the best known collections of Literary Chinese chuanqi tales from the Tang dynasty. The Taiping Guangji later preserved the whole corpus of these Tang tales.

The Classic of Poetry was already ancient by the Tang era, yet it was still being officially reworked. In 653 CE the Right Meaning of the Mao Poetry, built on Zheng Xuan's edition of the Mao text, became the imperially authorized text and commentary.
tags: Right Meaning of the Mao Poetry

literature.text: Gufeng, or "ancient airs", is a poetry genre modeled on the Airs section of the Shijing. Li Bo wrote a gufeng on Mount Taibai and also a poem titled 古風, showing the old anthology still inspiring Tang poets.

Du Fu wrote poems in the midst of the An Lushan rebellion. They are seen as a vital forerunner of the sangluan genre, a verse of death and destruction that dwells on the devastation of war, its death and disorder, and the violent, tumultuous events of the Yuan dynasty's founding by Kublai Khan. Yuan Haowen, a poet of both the Jin and Yuan dynasties, wrote notable examples.

Finest Flowers from the World of Letters is a 10th-century compilation of earlier works. It belongs to the tradition of Chinese fiction that grew out of narratives, official histories and less formal writings.
tags: Finest Flowers from the World of Letters

literature.text: The Book of Sui, completed in 636, was the first document to name Liu Yiqing as author of the You Ming Lu. Yet Shen Yue's earlier biography of Liu in the Book of Song never mentions the work, and Lu Xun argued Liu was its compiler rather than its author.

science.text: Sun Simiao, a Chinese physician known as China's King of Medicine, wrote two milestone medical books, Beiji Qianjin Yaofang and Qian Jin Yi Fang, listing about 5,300 and 2,000 recipes for medicines. Together the two books summarized medicine from before the Tang dynasty.

Li Chunfeng was a Chinese astronomer, mathematician, and historian who served as director of the Tang dynasty's Imperial Astronomical Bureau. He reformed the imperial calendar and annotated the classical Chinese mathematical canon.

Yi Xing, an eighth-century Buddhist monk astronomer of the Tang dynasty, built a celestial globe powered by a liquid-driven escapement. It was the first in a long tradition of Chinese astronomical clockworks.

A copy of the Tang dynasty Diamond Sutra, dated May 11, 868 CE and discovered among the Dunhuang manuscripts, is widely considered the oldest surviving printed book. Its closing colophon states it was created 'for universal free distribution.'

Sun Simiao's essay 'On the Absolute Sincerity of Great Physicians,' often called the Chinese Hippocratic Oath, forms the first chapter of his book Beiji Qianjin Yaofang. It is still required reading for Chinese physicians today.
tags: On the Absolute Sincerity of Great Physicians

science.text: In the early eighth century, the Tang court put Yi Xing in charge of an astrogeodetic survey to gather new astronomical data. The survey aimed to help predict solar eclipses and correct flaws in the existing calendar.

Sun Simiao experimented in Daoist external alchemy, and his Danjing Yaojue ('Essential Formulas of Alchemical Classics') is described by the sinologist Nathan Sivin as being as close to a modern laboratory handbook as anything in ancient literature, with detailed laboratory specifications including the 'six-one' lute used to seal reaction vessels. He believed deeply that alchemical elixirs would help humans achieve immortality. A tenth-century historian wrote that his body did not decay for some time after his death, due to the amount of mercury he ingested while trying to develop the perfect elixir of immortality.

After criticizing the outdated equipment of the Imperial Astronomy Bureau, Li Chunfeng was ordered to build a new armillary sphere, which he completed in 633. His design added a third ring beyond the standard two-ring design used before.

In 656, Li Chunfeng and his collaborators Liang Shu and Wang Zhenru compiled the Ten Mathematical Manuals, a set of ten classical mathematics texts submitted to the emperor. The collection became the standard curriculum for Tang state mathematics education.

politics.text: In 581 Emperor Wen founded the Sui dynasty in succession to the Northern Zhou. In 589 the Sui conquered the Southern Chen and reunified China, ending three centuries of political division.

After centuries of disunity, imperial unity was restored by the Sui dynasty (581–618) and then the Tang dynasty (618–907). The Tang is remembered as a golden age of poetry, culture and cosmopolitan trade.
During the Tang dynasty, China achieved a golden age in economic, military and political power. Tang territory spanned Central Asia, Northeast Asia and parts of Southeast Asia.

The Song dynasty began in 960, when Emperor Taizu of Song usurped the throne of the Later Zhou dynasty. He went on to conquer the rest of the Ten Kingdoms, ending the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period.

The short-lived Sui pioneered the government system of Three Departments and Six Ministries. It also used imperial examinations to select officials from commoners, and improved the fubing conscription system and the equal-field land distribution system. Later dynasties adopted these policies.

Sui China was known for mega-construction projects. The Grand Canal was built to ship grain and troops, linking the capitals Daxing (Chang'an) and Luoyang to the wealthy southeast and, by another route, to the northeast border. The Great Wall was also expanded.

The Sui invasions of the Korean Peninsula in the Goguryeo–Sui War failed disastrously. They triggered widespread revolts that led to the fall of the dynasty, even though the Sui had pacified its borders with military conquests and diplomatic maneuvers.
Under the Sui, standardized coinage was enforced throughout the unified empire. Buddhism took root as a prominent religion and was supported officially by the state.
During the Northern Song, which began in 960, the capital was the northern city of Bianjing, now Kaifeng. From there the dynasty controlled most of what is now East China.

philosophy.text: Buddhism became a unifying cultural force in China during a time of limited central political control. It lifted people out of war and into the Sui dynasty, and in many ways was responsible for the rebirth of culture under the Sui.

The Tang dynasty recognized and protected three Iranian religions: Zoroastrianism, the Church of the East, and Manichaeism. Known as the three Persian religions, they prospered in China while Sassanid Iran was falling to the early Muslim conquests.

During the late Six dynasties and Sui dynasty, local Chinese schools of Buddhist thought started to flourish. Early Buddhist teachings had been acquired from Sanskrit sutras, but Chinese thinkers now began to build their own traditions.

Emperor Wen and his empress converted to Buddhism to legitimise imperial authority over China and the conquest of Chen. The emperor presented himself as a Cakravartin king, a Buddhist monarch who would use military force to defend the Buddhist faith.

The Confucian philosopher Wang Tong wrote and taught during the Sui dynasty and briefly held office as Secretary of Shuzhou. His most famous work, and the only one to survive, is the Explanation of the Mean, compiled shortly after his death in 617.

According to a tablet, in 635 Alopen came to Chang'an with scriptures. Emperor Taizong sent his chancellor Fang Xuanling to welcome him, and after examining the teachings ordered a temple built and the scriptures translated.

Zhiyi founded the Tiantai school and completed the Great treatise on Concentration and Insight. In it he taught the principle of "Three Thousand Realms in a Single moment of Life" as the essence of Buddhist teaching outlined in the Lotus Sutra.

Emperor Wen and his empress converted to Buddhism to legitimise imperial authority over China and the conquest of Chen. He presented himself as a Cakravartin king, a Buddhist monarch who would use military force to defend the Buddhist faith. In 601 AD he had relics of the Buddha distributed to temples throughout China, with edicts hoping that all people within the Four Seas would develop enlightenment and cultivate fortunate karma. The article calls this act an imitation of the ancient Mauryan Emperor Ashoka of India.

The Sui court also pursued a pro-Taoist policy. The first reign of the dynasty promoted the Northern Louguan school of Taoism, while the second reign promoted the Southern Shangqing school, possibly due to Emperor Yang's preference for Southern culture.

The Church of the East was first called the Great Qin Church and the Persian Scripture Church, because its seat was in the Sassanid Empire. It developed smoothly in China for 150 years, and it was said that the temples filled a hundred cities.

Zoroastrianism, one of the three Persian religions, was targeted in the mid-800s during the Huichang persecution of Buddhism under Emperor Wuzong of Tang. It eventually disappeared in China after the fall of the Song dynasty in 1279.

The Persian monk Jingjing is said to have translated 35 Jing sutras into Chinese in the 8th century. The Jing religion declined rapidly when Emperor Wu Zong of the Tang initiated the Huichang persecution of Buddhism.

The three Persian religions were persecuted in the 9th century during the Huichang Persecution of Buddhism, which led to their gradual decline. Manichaeism later passed into folk secrets, blending with Buddhism, Taoism, and folk beliefs.

culture.text: During the Tang dynasty, Buddhism became the predominant religion for the common people. The capital, Chang'an (modern Xi'an), was the largest city in the world of its time. The era is remembered as a golden age of poetry, culture and cosmopolitan trade.

Chinese tea culture emerged in the Tang dynasty and flourished in later eras as a major cultural practice and export good. Japanese Buddhist monks who visited China during the Tang returned home with tea. Saichō is recorded as the first to cultivate tea in Japan, planting it on Mt Hiei.

The three Persian religions, Zoroastrianism, the Church of the East and Manichaeism, were recognized and protected under Tang rule. They prospered as Sassanid Iran fell to the early Muslim conquests. In the 9th century the Huichang Persecution of Buddhism led to their gradual decline.
Two Japanese monks are named as key figures in bringing Chinese tea to Japan. Saichō stayed at Fulong Temple on Mount Tai, while Kūkai stayed at Ximing Temple in Chang'an.

Buddhism first arrived in China as a kind of "foreign Taoism", and its scriptures were translated using Taoist vocabulary. In the Tang period, Taoism in turn took on Buddhist elements such as monasteries, vegetarianism and a prohibition of alcohol. Chan Buddhism grew to become the largest sect in Chinese Buddhism.

In 635, according to a stele, the Church of the East's Alopen came to Chang'an, the Tang capital, bringing scriptures. Emperor Taizong sent his chancellor Fang Xuanling to welcome him and ordered a temple built in Yiningfang. The faith developed smoothly for 150 years.

Tang authorities regarded Manichaeism, which arrived through Central Asian communities, as an improper form of Buddhism. Religions of Western peoples were not outlawed, but they were prohibited from spreading among the native Chinese population. Even so, Manichaeism was a popular faith in northern China during the Tang.
The earliest evidence of Christianity in China dates to the eighth century. It is a stone stele in Xi'an inscribed with a summary of basic Nestorian teachings.

In 731, Emperor Xuanzong of Tang asked a Manichaean to summarize their foreign doctrines. The result was the Compendium of the Teachings of Mani, the Awakened One of Light, which presents Mani as an incarnation of Laozi. An 8th-century version of the Taoist Huahujing shares this view.
The most complete set of surviving Manichaean writings was written in Chinese before the 9th century. These texts were found in the Mogao Caves among the Dunhuang manuscripts.
